summary: Offers one possible plan for moving the Internet from mostly IPv4 connectivity to mostly IPv6 connectivity. It is a proposal, not a decision of the IETF, and is informational.

eli5.summary: Switching the whole internet to new addresses is like moving a city to a new street system. This paper offers one plan for doing it step by step.

questions: internet transition plan ipv4 to ipv6
how to move from ipv4 to ipv6
subtitle: A phased timeline for transitioning the Internet from IPv4 to IPv6

tldr.problem: The Internet is running out of IPv4 addresses, and switching to IPv6 requires coordination across millions of independent networks and organizations with different capabilities and timelines.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5211 proposes a three-phase plan: preparation (2009), transition (2010–2011), and post-transition (2012 onward), assigning specific roles and expectations to service providers and end-site organizations in each phase.
tldr.outcome: The plan aims to ensure continuous Internet connectivity during the migration by setting clear expectations and allowing enough time for each actor to adapt, though it is a proposal, not an IETF standard or mandate.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Informational proposal, not an IETF standard

today: RFC 5211 is a historical planning document. The Internet's actual IPv6 transition proceeded more slowly than the 2008 timeline projected. As of 2026, IPv4 addresses have been exhausted in most regions (APNIC in 2011, RIPE in 2012, LACNIC in 2014, ARIN in 2015), but dual-stack remains the norm, and IPv6 adoption, while steadily increasing, has not reached the post-transition dominance RFC 5211 envisioned. The document remains valuable as a reference for how large-scale infrastructure transitions are proposed and coordinated.

sections.title: The IPv4 Address Crisis and the Need for a Plan
sections.content:
IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, giving the Internet about 4.3 billion unique addresses. By 2008, when RFC 5211 was published, the growth of mobile devices, IoT, and cloud computing was rapidly consuming remaining addresses, with exhaustion projected within a few years.

IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses—enough to give every grain of sand on Earth its own address. But IPv6 is fundamentally incompatible with IPv4. Switching the entire Internet is one of the largest infrastructure migrations in history.

RFC 5211 emphasizes that this document is a proposal and informational RFC, not an IETF mandate. Different regions, operators, and organizations will transition at different rates. The goal is to publish a plausible plan that demonstrates the transition is feasible and to coordinate expectations to maintain universal Internet connectivity throughout.
sections.eli5: The old address system is almost full. A new one is ready but completely different. We need a plan so people switch at about the same pace and the Internet does not break.

sections.title: Preparation Phase (2009)
sections.content:
In the Preparation Phase, service providers begin piloting IPv6 services, and organizations enable IPv6 on public-facing servers (those visible to the Internet) while keeping IPv4.

The plan expects: Service providers SHOULD pilot IPv6, using either native IPv6 networks or transition mechanisms (like IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels). Organizations SHOULD arrange IPv6 connectivity for servers like web, email, and DNS servers, ideally using separate service names to avoid disrupting existing IPv4 customers. Organizations MAY provide IPv6 to internal users (optional in this phase).

The Preparation Phase allows organizations to gain experience, test their systems, and prepare infrastructure without forcing immediate change. It is not required to be production-ready; pilot status is acceptable.
sections.eli5: Phase 1: Try it out. Set up IPv6 systems, test them, but keep running IPv4 as usual. No one has to commit yet.

sections.title: Transition Phase (2010–2011)
sections.content:
In the Transition Phase, the stakes increase. Service providers MUST offer IPv6 as a production service (native IPv6 is preferred, but transition mechanisms are acceptable). Organizations MUST arrange IPv6 for public-facing servers, and IPv6 services should now be treated as production-quality by both the organization and by others consuming those services.

Additionally, organizations SHOULD provide IPv6 to internal user communities and internal supporting infrastructure like DNS and DHCP servers (with either native IPv6 or transition mechanisms).

This phase marks the shift from optional experimentation to mandatory deployment. The plan expects most public-facing infrastructure to be reachable via IPv6 by 2011, ensuring that organizations entering the post-transition phase can rely on significant IPv6 coverage.
sections.eli5: Phase 2: Go live. All big services must work on IPv6 and be treated as production. Organizations that need IPv6-only connections will be able to reach most of the web.

sections.title: Post-Transition Phase (2012 Onward)
sections.content:
In the Post-Transition Phase, the Internet is predominantly IPv6. Organizations MUST provide IPv6 for public-facing servers and MUST treat IPv6 as production. New customers can now be issued only IPv6 addresses and expect to reach nearly all public services.

Service providers MUST offer IPv6 connectivity, with native IPv6 as the default. Organizations SHOULD (but are not required to) provide IPv6 internally as well.

IPv4 is not abandoned: POST4 allows service providers and organizations to continue offering and using IPv4 service indefinitely. Dual-stack (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6) becomes the long-term reality.

The timeline sets January 2012 as the target for this phase, chosen to arrive before IPv4 address exhaustion projections. This ensures that pure-IPv6 customers can still reach a mature ecosystem of IPv6-enabled services.
sections.eli5: Phase 3: IPv6 is the default. If you are a new company, you can get an IPv6-only internet connection and reach most of the web. Old IPv4 networks still exist but are no longer required.

sections.title: The Key Insight: Public-Facing Servers First
sections.content:
RFC 5211's central insight is that adding IPv6 to public-facing servers is easier than transitioning an entire organization. A small team can enable IPv6 on a web server without changing internal networks. This is far less work than retrofitting an organization's entire infrastructure.

By requiring public-facing IPv6 in the Transition Phase, the plan creates an environment where post-transition IPv6-only customers have access to a critical mass of services. This economic incentive helps pull the Internet toward IPv6 adoption.

The RFC notes this is still a significant hurdle: organizations lack immediate financial incentives to upgrade, and RFC 5211 ultimately depends on a shared commitment among Internet participants that "connectivity is its own reward"—the belief that a connected, functioning Internet benefits everyone enough to justify the upgrade burden.
sections.eli5: The clever part: If you only have to fix your public website (not your whole company), you will probably do it. Once enough websites support IPv6, new companies can use only IPv6.
